document.title: Simple Task / Wait Coordination System
document.purpose: Describe a minimal, append-friendly task system and define the soft structure of a task record.
author: Lion Kimbro
Wing-Cat

overview.description: This project defines a simple, file-friendly task coordination system. Tasks are represented as JSON dictionaries. Updates may be written as partial records, allowing append-only logs and multi-program interaction.
core-ideas: Each task is identified by a UUID.
Each record is a dictionary that may partially update a task.
Records include a timestamp (`ts`) indicating when the record was created.
Tasks include a `created_at` field indicating when the task itself was created.
Priority is relative to the project context.
Urgency is derived from deadline and estimated effort, not stored.
The system is designed to be simple, human-writable, and compatible with programmatic use.
core-principles: This system is append-only and record-based.
Tasks are never mutated directly; all changes are expressed as records.
Current task state is derived by replaying records in timestamp order.

notes: This system is conceptually aligned with M1 (entities and aspects), but does not require M1 transport format.
Each task is an entity identified by a UUID.
Each JSON record is an assertion about that entity.
Latest values (by timestamp) determine current state.
History may be preserved by storing all records.

uuid.description: A globally unique identifier in hyphenated UUID format (8-4-4-4-12).
notes: This is the standard hyphenated UUID representation.
Other identifier forms (e.g., tag URIs) are not included in this type.
Tools may validate the pattern, but are not required to enforce it.

task-record.title: Task Record
task-record.description: A task record is a JSON object representing either a full task or a partial update to a task.

ts.description: Time when this record (update) was created.

created_at.description: Time when the task itself was originally created. Typically only set on initial creation.

title.description: Short human-readable description of the task.

vocabulary.ACTIVE: Task is actionable now; it is currently the actor's responsibility to work on it.
vocabulary.WAITING: Task is explicitly deferred. The actor is not currently responsible for it. Waiting may be time-based (a wait_until date is set, and the task becomes actionable when that date arrives) or dependency-based (waiting on another person, an event, or an external condition, with no specific date). WAITING is a meaningful status distinct from ACTIVE: it expresses that the task has been consciously set aside, not forgotten.
vocabulary.CANCELED: Task was deliberately dropped by an intentional decision. The actor chose to stop pursuing it.
vocabulary.EXPIRED: The window for action on this task closed without the task being completed. A passive terminal state: the opportunity lapsed rather than being deliberately abandoned. Distinct from CANCELED in cause — CANCELED reflects a decision, EXPIRED reflects a missed window.

notes: WAITING vs ACTIVE+wait_until: a task may be ACTIVE and carry a wait_until date as a reminder, but WAITING explicitly signals that the task is not currently the actor's responsibility. WAITING is the correct status when the actor has consciously handed off, deferred, or blocked the task.
EXPIRED is a terminal state like DONE and CANCELED. It should not be automatically assigned by the system; it is set explicitly when the actor recognises that the opportunity has lapsed.
CANCELED and EXPIRED are both non-completion terminals, but carry different meaning in history: CANCELED means 'I chose not to do this', EXPIRED means 'I did not get to this in time'.

project.description: Reference to the project or context this task belongs to.

uuid.description: Strong identifier for the project (if known).

tag.description: Lightweight tag used as project reference.

notes: The project reference may be partially specified.
It is valid to include only a tag, name, or UUID.
Resolvers may later map name or tag to a UUID.
This allows tasks to be created cheaply and refined over time.
Priority is conceptually an integer from 1 to 5.
JSON requires object keys to be strings, but these values should be interpreted numerically.
Priority is ordinal (tiered), not a precise scalar.
Priority is meaningful only within the context of a project.

deadline.description: Time by which the task should be completed.

wait_until.description: If WAITING due to time, when the task becomes actionable.

estimate_hours.description: Estimated effort required to complete the task.

logged_hours.description: Total amount of time spent on the task so far.
notes: This value represents a cumulative total, not a delta.
Changes over time may be inferred by comparing values across records.
This field is optional but recommended when tracking effort.

tags.description: Additional labels for filtering and grouping the task.

comment.description: A note about this specific record (update), describing why the change was made or what happened at this time.
examples: Correcting status from DONE back to ACTIVE
notes: This is not a persistent note about the task itself.
It is associated with the record timestamp (`ts`) and reflects the context of this specific update.
Multiple comments may exist across different records for the same task.
Comments are not merged into task state; they are part of the task's history.

by.description: Identifier of the author (human or program) making this record.

uuid.description: Strong identifier for the entity (person or program), if known.

person.description: Human-readable name of the person making the record.

program.description: Name of the program generating the record.

notes: The UUID is preferred when available, as it provides stable identity.
The 'person' and 'program' fields provide lightweight identification when a UUID is not available.
This structure mirrors the 'project' reference pattern: start simple, refine later.

resources.description: A list of external resources associated with the task, such as folders, files, or URLs.

items.description: A reference to a resource relevant to the task.

uuid.description: UUID for the resource being referenced.

notes: Used when the resource refers to a local file or folder.
Interpretation of the path is environment-dependent.

title.description: Optional human-readable label for the resource.

notes: The structure is intentionally flexible; additional keys may be included as needed.
Different resource types may use different fields (e.g., 'path' for local resources, 'url' for web resources).
Consumers should interpret fields based on the 'resource' type.
Not all fields are required; partial descriptions are acceptable.
A record may include all fields (full snapshot) or only a subset (partial update).
Partial updates override previous values for specified fields.
Unspecified fields remain unchanged when reconstructing task state.
Urgency is not stored. It is computed from deadline and estimate_hours.
Next-task selection is based on project importance, priority, and urgency.
WAITING tasks may be surfaced based on wait_until and elapsed time.
A WAITING task whose wait_until has passed is 'expired-wait': it should be visually flagged as ready to activate, but its status remains WAITING until the actor explicitly changes it.

EXPIRED (the status) is distinct from an expired wait_until. An expired wait_until means the wait period has ended and the task is ready to activate. EXPIRED (status) means the task itself is permanently closed because its window has passed.
System behavior emerges from interpretation of records, not rigid structure.

merge-method.description: Defines how multiple task records are combined to produce the current state of each task.
core-rule: Records are processed in ascending order of `ts` (timestamp).
For each task (`id`), later records overwrite earlier values for the same field.
The current state of a task is the result of applying all its records in time order.

steps: Load all records from all input sources (e.g., JSONL files).
Sort all records by `ts` in ascending order.
Iterate through each record in order.
For each record, locate or create the task state for its `id`.
For each key in the record (except `id` and `ts`), assign the value to the task state.
Continue until all records have been processed.

notes: Fields are overwritten by later records (latest value wins).
id is used to identify the task and is always present in the resulting task object.  It is not derived from field merging.
`ts` is a record-level field and is not merged into task state.
`comment` is a record-level field and is not merged into task state.
`created_at` should be set once and not overwritten if already present.
Fields not mentioned in a record remain unchanged in the task state.
Object-valued fields (e.g., `project`, `by`) are replaced as a whole; no deep merge is performed.
Setting a field to `null` may be used in the future to indicate clearing a value, but this behavior is not required initially.
If desired, all records may be retained to preserve full history.
A history view may be constructed by grouping records by `id` and preserving their order.
Snapshots of task state may be stored or cached for convenience.
The canonical behavior of the system is defined by replaying records.
Snapshots, when used, should be treated as derived views and may be recomputed.
This method is intentionally simple and deterministic.
It supports append-only storage and multi-source input without coordination.
It is compatible with both human-written and program-generated records.
More advanced behaviors (e.g., conflict resolution, partial object merging) are intentionally omitted to preserve simplicity.
